author: reek
body: Until 2026-07-28 those three read "the signature we can check, the curve we cannot, and the digest we have not implemented", and this file's recorded answers were the shape of what was missing: the root parsed as `ecdsa-other` with can-verify False, and `inter signed by root` was False. All three are implemented now and both lines changed -- the root is `ecdsa-p384`, and the intermediate verifies against it under SHA-384. **The chain that motivated the work now checks end to end**, which is the only reason to believe the P-384 and SHA-384 code does what its own unit tests say it does.

author: reek
body: The positive was confirmed against TWO independent implementations before any of the code below was written: OpenSSL 3.2.4, verifying the leaf against the intermediate as a partial trust anchor, and .NET's ECDsa on Windows CNG, verifying the sliced tbsCertificate directly. Both also reject every perturbation here. A transcription error in these fixtures has somewhere to show up, which a single-oracle check could not offer.

author: reek
body: THESE CERTIFICATES WILL EXPIRE AND THIS TEST WILL NOT NOTICE, on the same reasoning RealCertTest sets out: a signature does not expire, and this chapter asks only whether these bytes were signed by that key.

author: reek
body: The DER decoder next, and the trailing byte is the case that matters. A signature with a byte appended decodes to exactly the same r and s, so without the whole-buffer check it verifies and NO end-to-end line anywhere would move. Every other rejection the decoder can make is one the arithmetic would also make.

author: reek
body: An r whose top byte has the sign bit set with no zero in front of it is a negative DER INTEGER, which no ECDSA component ever is.

author: reek
body: An r of thirty-three significant bytes is not a scalar on this curve.
